Core concepts explored in this unit include membrane transport, protein sorting and maturation, protein degradation, vesicle trafficking and fundamental concepts of cell signalling. The laboratories reinforce lecture concepts and enable students to develop biological laboratory skills

title: Frontiers in Cell Biology
description: In this unit students will study advanced cell biology concepts and techniques, building on knowledge acquired in Foundations of Cell Biology. Advanced topics covered in this unit include developmental and stem cell biology, cell biology of aging, cell therapies and tissue engineering, organelle dependent signalling and dynamics, regulation of gene expression, nutrient and energy regulated signalling, the life cycle of cells and the cell biology of cancer and disease.

title: Exercise Physiology, Nutrition and Performance
description: Nutrition and exercise physiology are naturally linked. This unit will build on previously learnt concepts to explore aspects of nutrition and physiology that facilitate exercise performance. Through a combination of lectures and practical classes, students will develop an understanding and appreciation for the human physiological response and adaptation to physical activity, in the context of physical performance, environmental stress, energy balance and health.

title: Nutritional Physiology
description: This unit will build on previously learnt concepts to explore aspects of physiology that support the study of nutrition. Through a combination of lectures and practical classes, students will develop an understanding and appreciation for human body function, with focus on the central theme of homeostasis

title: Animal Production
description: Scientific principles (biochemical, anatomical and physiological) that underpin intensive and extensive animal production. These principles will be related to key production parameters and indicators including growth, reproduction, lactation and milk production, fibre production and breeding. Students will apply the scientific principles to planning of production in farming simulation models.

title: Physics of Stars and Galaxies
description: This unit begins with an overview of basic cosmology, applying Newtonian physics to understand the observational consequences of the hot Big Bang and the theory of inflation, from the expansion of the Universe to the existence and properties of the Cosmic Microwave background and the abundances of light elements. The physics of stars is then explored in some detail, from stellar structure to the nuclear reactions that produce energy, showing that stellar nucleosynthesis and supernova explosions generate all the heavy elements in the universe. Stellar life cycles are then investigated, from star formation to stellar end products (white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes), exploring in detail the use of star clusters (both open and globular) as evolutionary microcsoms. Galactic structure and dynamics are then discussed, leading into an exploration of some key issues in modern astrophysical research, such as dark matter problem. Finally, the understanding of Galactic structure and accretion physics gained in this unit is applied to explore the nature of quasars, the most luminous objects in the Universe that are powered by super-massive black holes in the cores of galaxies.

title: Property Construction
description: Students in this unit will develop their understanding of the property and construction industry in Australia. This includes interpreting building life cycle decisions for climate adaptation, sustainable property practices towards a low carbon economy that incorporate indigenous cultural awareness and workplace equality and diversity. Statutory requirements, building regulations and environmental considerations form an integral part of the unit. Students will learn and apply building measurement and costing techniques using real world examples.

title: Advanced Cropping System Technologies Project
description: This unit will provide students with practical and theoretical knowledge of new technologies associated with broadacre cropping and pastures, and their role in crop focused and mixed farming systems. The course will focus primarily on advanced agronomy to contribute to more productive and sustainable land management systems and will also draw on the practical application of soil and crop management and plant breeding approaches from other units. The advanced agronomy component will explore elements of successful crop management, recognizing variability in performance within the paddock and farm, diagnosing the underlying causes of spatial and temporal variability, and using digital agriculture tools to improve enterprise management decisions, plant yield and quality for end users. Student projects including project design, management and analysis, will be an integral component of the unit. These elements will be developed against the background of climate change and other drivers for farming systems in the future.

title: Architecture and Interior Architecture Methods 1A - Analogue Literacy
description: This unit introduces students to ways in which designers communicate aspects of the built environment through the exploration of a design problem. The emphasis is on the importance of the visualisation of concepts for a sketch design and design development. The syllabus includes introduction and application of scale and analogue techniques, including observation, hand drawn sketching, diagramming, and orthographic projection and modelling techniques.

title: Foundations of Biology
description: This unit explores the diversity and evolution of life from the molecular to the ecosystem level. Students completing this unit will develop an integrated understanding of the structure and function of organisms, and will explore how reproduction and inheritance form the bias of evolution and biological diversity. Students will develop theoretical and practical skills in experimental design, problem solving, data analysis, and communication necessary to study complex biological systems and the processes of organisation, regulation and response that shape those systems.

title: Practical Consumer and Competition Law
description: This unit provides the students with a business focused exploration of laws that impact on customers and competitors. The legal risks arising from the Australian Competition and Consumer Law, on business actions and strategies including misleading or deceptive conduct, unfair sales techniques, pricing strategies, consumer guarantees, selling strategies and collusion are analysed in the context of the legal impact on a business, its directors, management and staff.

title: Understanding Biotechnology
description: Exploration of the biotechnology industry, beginning with traditional forms and recent developments in biotechnology. Examination of how biological processes can be harnessed to perform or supplement technical processes, including their role in developing renewable and sustainable systems for agriculture and industry. Overview of the contemporary biotechnology industry and applications of iopharmaceuticals, transgenics, genomics, proteomics and monoclonal antibody technology, DNA and protein analysis as diagnostic tools, and rational drug design. Comparisons are made between the biotechnology industries in a selection of different countries. Principles are studied for the objective assessment of positive or negative claims and arguments about biotechnology which can be applied equally to other areas of science. Assessments assist in decision-making and development of skills for writing clear and precise scientific documents.

title: Research Skills for Biomedical Sciences
description: In this unit, students will continue their journey to becoming biomedical science researchers gaining introductory skills and practical experience enabling them to understand how to apply research methods to evaluate the body of evidence in biomedicine. The unit will commence with an introduction to scientific methods, where practical experience in the development of research questions, research ethics, regulatory consideration, and risk management will be undertaken. This will be complemented by further development of skills in scientific reading and writing, where students will learn how to identify and critically review literature and write scientifically for disparate audience. The art of critical thinking, data analysis and presentation skills will also be introduced. Students will be exposed to authentic research activities and will begin to develop leadership and entrepreneurial skills.

title: Biosciences Research Project
description: In this unit students will be provided with an introduction to research within the Biosciences. The unit will focus on the philosophy of science, research design, ethical conduct, critical analysis of the relevant scientific literature to develop a literature review, hypothesis and aims, data collection and analysis and reporting.

title: Specialised Construction
description: In this unit, students will examine advanced techniques and methodologies used in construction works, such as deep excavations, basement construction, dewatering, retaining walls, soil stabilisation, underpinning, structural concrete, temporary support and demolition.

title: Construction Planning and Scheduling
description: This unit enables students to develop construction planning and scheduling skills. Students will learn the concepts of planning and scheduling, such as the critical path method (CPM), understand the procedures for creating schedules for construction projects, learn how to use CPM in construction projects to support resource management, cash flow analysis, project progress monitoring and control, and 4D simulation.

title: Construction Estimating and Cost Planning
description: In this unit, students will develop estimating skills and strategic estimating methods in buildings. The estimating strategies will align and apply into the processes of design economics, cost benefit analysis and elemental cost analysis at the early stage of project development.

title: Introduction to Management in Construction
description: This unit will provide students with an overview of the construction industry, project life cycle, the industry’s place in the community and external factors that influence it. The role, functions, and professional practices of construction managers, quantity surveyors and project managers will be discussed. Students will be introduced to a range of management concepts and techniques associated with construction projects.

title: Integrated Construction Project 1
description: This unit integrates academic learning with its application in the workplace, using a simulated virtual project or an authentic project in the workplace. Students will work in a collaborative construction environment to apply and evaluate innovative practices in strategic management, project planning, design, procurement and construction processes.

title: Biomolecular Structure and Interactions
description: This unit emphasises protein and nucleic acid structure, dynamics and interactions. This unit explores topics such as biomolecular interactions, hierarchy of protein and nucleic acid structures, experimental and theoretical methods to study protein structure and interactions, molecular modelling of biomolecular structure and interactions, protein folding, visualization of biomolecular structure. This emphasis on protein and nucleic acid structure and interactions reflects the crucial importance of these biomolecules to life.

title: Process Safety and Risk Management
description: This unit introduces students to the practice of process safety and risk management as it is performed in the engineering sectors of process industries. Fundamental hazards, process risk and safety concepts, and systematic risk assessment methods are discussed. Historical accident scenarios are reviewed to help students gain an appreciation for the complexities involved in understanding, managing and mitigating risks in the process industries. Students need to apply different measures, i.e., qualitative, semi-quantitative, and quantitative techniques, to process hazard and risk, as well as risks related to renewable energy, environmental management and sustainability. Risk management across the life cycle of a process system is explored, in conjunction with inherently safer design principles, risk assessments and mitigations. Key methods around hazard identification, consequence modelling and likelihood estimation, as precursors for estimating risk, are thoroughly examined as a central part of process safety and risk management practice. Emerging process risk management in high-pressure gas/liquid storage, renewable energy applications, sustainability, etc., are covered in this unit. Broader issues around process safety management systems, human factors, complex systems, pressure vessels, resilience engineering and regulatory matters are also considered.

title: Mass and Energy Balances
description: This unit introduces students to one of the most fundamental, useful and important tools that chemical and process engineers use: material and energy balances. They help us understand, analyse, design, troubleshoot and optimise industrial processes that involve physical changes and chemical transformations. Students are taken through the following topics: Introductory Concepts (dimensions, systems of units, basis of calculations, moles and concentrations); Material Balances without Reaction; Flow Diagrams; Material Balances involving Reactions; Material Balance for Combustion Systems; Multi-unit Systems (including recycle, bypass and purge); Industrial Applications; Material Balances involving Ideal Gases; Multiphase Equilibrium; Energy Balances (terminology and types of energy); Energy Balances without Reaction; Energy Balances accounting for Chemical Reaction (heat of formation, heat of reaction, sensible and latent heats, heat of combustion); Combined Material and Energy Balances. The unit provides an insight into the way chemical engineers approach problems and supplies concepts that underlie many other study units in the curriculum.

title: Advanced Particle Processes
description: Introduction to Particle Processes. Properties and Sampling of Particulate Solids. Nanoparticles and Nanotechnology: nanoporous materials; synthesis of nanomaterials; characteristics of nanomaterials; applications of nanomaterials. The Motion of Particles: fundamental physical processes; particle-particle interactions; particle packing; particles in fluids, fixed beds and fluidized beds. Particle Characterisation: particle adhesion and crystallisation; particle size measurement and analysis. Catalysts and Heterogeneous Catalysis. Particle Handling and Processing: mixing of particles, particle agglomeration / granulation and coagulation processes; froth flotation; particle modelling in particulate processes. Environment and Safety: comminution and environmental considerations; dust explosion hazard assessment and control.

title: Electrochemical Energy Conversion and Storage
description: This unit discusses the applications of electrochemical energy storage and conversion. The students will be introduced to the practical aspects of electrochemistry, during which their previous knowledge of thermodynamics, kinetics and mass transport will be applied to electrochemical systems. Based on these electrochemical principles, an overview of electrochemical energy storage and conversion systems will be provided, including batteries, supercapacitors, electrolysers, and fuel cells.

title: Computational Fluid Dynamics
description: Basic concepts of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD); FLUENT and GAMBIT software; Conservation partial differential equations and their solution using finite volume.

title: Chemical Engineering Design Project
description: The Chemical Engineering Design Project is the capstone unit of the course - it relies on, reinforces and applies many of the principles and techniques learnt in previous units. In the first part of the semester, students work in groups to research and perform a realistic, open-ended chemical plant design study at the flow-sheet level. This involves performing a market survey; identifying, evaluating and selecting suitable process technologies; adapting or synthesising a process flowsheet; assessing and choosing a site location; generating and optimising mass and energy balances for the process flowsheet; performing preliminary equipment and piping design; developing a plant-wide process control philosophy with consideration of plant start-up and shutdown; initial evaluation and mitigation of safety and environmental impacts; creating a plant layout and plot plan; estimating capital and operating costs, and making a preliminary assessment of economic feasibility with scenario and sensitivity analyses. In the second part of the semester, students work individually to conduct detailed design studies on two equipment systems in their plant, covering process, operational and mechanical design aspects, including a critical review of their final designs.

title: Reactivity and Function in Chemistry
description: This unit is designed for students who have passed CHEM1000 Principles and Processes in Chemistry or CHEM1001 Biological Chemistry. This unit will prepare you for a wide array of future careers by illustrating how an understanding of reactivity and function assists understanding biological, medicinal, geological and industrial processes. It will provide you with the skills to predict reactions of common functional groups by demonstrating how the mechanistic process gives the outcomes of new, but related reactions, including reactions of relevance to your chosen discipline. Chemical reactions occur over a very wide range of timescales and the ability to measure and predict the rates of reaction, particularly as they are influenced by a number of factors, will display how this has direct influence on your everyday life. Finally, dynamic systems in biology, medicine, industry and nature will illustrate the importance of chemical equilibria.

title: Materials Selection and Corrosion
description: This unit explains the gradual degradation of engineering materials in various environments. In particular, the fundamentals of electrochemistry will be introduced to explain corrosion processes of metallic materials. Application of electrochemical techniques to monitor and quantify corrosion of metallic materials. Various corrosive environments such as in oil and gas exploration and production, offshore windfarms, etc. will be discussed. Industry standards related to material selection and corrosion control strategies will be introduced.

title: Building Services
description: This unit discusses the essential role that building services play in enabling buildings to provide functional and comfortable living and working areas. Cost implications of service installations for construction projects are discussed. Students will explore the comfort and energy performance of buildings.

title: Thermodynamics
description: The objective of this unit is to learn the fundamentals of thermodynamics with the 1st and 2nd Laws, and apply them to relevant engineering situations. Non-ideality of gases and liquids is introduced via the compressibility factor, residual, and excess properties. The broader framework of solution thermodynamics, including phase equilibrium, focuses on vapour-liquid equilibrium and reaction equilibria. Maxwell's relations are used to derive property relations. Students also learn about heat engines for the production of power from heat, as well as refrigeration and liquefaction cycles. Finally, the thermodynamics of fuel cells are introduced.

title: Integrated Construction Project 2
description: In this unit students will demonstrate the integration of skills, knowledge tools and techniques learnt in the Construction Management course and application to practical problems in a cross-disciplinary context.

title: Exploring the Radio Universe
description: This unit begins with the fundamental principles of radio astronomy, following the signal chain of a single-dish radio telescope. Important concepts like antenna sensitivity patterns, receivers, frequency conversion and square-law detection are introduced. The techniques of radio interferometry and aperture synthesis are also explained from a mathematical viewpoint. Some time is spent describing the design of proposed next-generation radio telescopes, with particular reference to the square kilometre array. This unit also introduces the physical mechanisms by which astronomical radiation is generated at radio wavelengths and examines some of the astrophysical sources that can be studied using radio telescopes.

title: Communicating with China
description: This unit further develops intercultural communicative competence in the Chinese language through collaborative and self-directed learning activities. Students will acquire skills in handling short written texts on topics relating to contemporary Chinese society and culture. They will be encouraged to express opinions, conduct discussions and present reports. Relevant cultural and social issues related to the Chinese speaking communities will be explored and discussed.

title: Carbon Management
description: This unit aims to provide students with comprehensive knowledge and skills necessary to manage carbon emissions as a remedy for climate change and an essential building block for sustainable development in today’s industrial world. The unit sets the scene by defining the carbon cycle, greenhouse effect and climate change, carbon footprint, and the role of carbon management in upholding UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Subsequently, it presents a detailed technical overview of practical carbon control approaches, including carbon capture, utilisation and storage technologies, and the role of renewable energy and energy efficiency improvements. The unit also provides students with a well-rounded understanding of the challenges and opportunities in implementing carbon management strategies, including policies and regulations, corporate responsibility, emissions monitoring and reporting, and carbon trading and economics. The unit incorporates case studies and real-world examples to reinforce students’ comprehension of theoretical concepts covered.

title: Chinese Society and Culture
description: This unit provides insights into both the traditional and contemporary Chinese society and culture. It explores the causal factors that help shape China based on cultural artifacts and reflections. The philosophical and cultural underpinnings of various historical, social and cultural phenomena are examined. A cross-cultural comparative angle is adopted and critical thinking is promoted to enable deep thinking.

title: Chinese for Beginners
description: This unit introduces basic communicative skills in Mandarin Chinese at an elementary level. Students acquire the four essential language skills of speaking, listening, reading and writing through ample practice in communicative activities supported by digital technology. Students will also be introduced to Chinese society, Chinese culture and the structure of the Chinese language through mini-lectures, audio-visual presentations and real-time classroom-based or online tutorials.

title: Intermediate Chinese: Extending Everyday Contexts
description: Further develops communicative competence in the Chinese language through collaborative and self-directed learning activities. Students will acquire skills in handling short written texts on topics relating to contemporary Chinese society. They will be encouraged to express opinions, conduct discussions and present reports. Relevant cultural and social issues will be discussed.

title: Advanced Chinese: Cultural Connections
description: This unit is designed to further promote an understanding of cultural etiquettes and social behaviours in Chinese culture. The unit develops students' language skills through close reading of non-authentic and authentic texts in Chinese language. These skills would be demonstrated by application of complex vocabulary and grammatical techniques. Focus will also be on analysis and exploration of similarities and differences in social and cultural norms and communication patterns between Chinese and other cultures.

title: Foundations of Chinese
description: This unit covers both written and spoken Chinese at an introductory level that builds on prior knowledge gained in CHIN1000. A communication-oriented approach is used to help students develop confidence in speaking, listening, reading and writing Standard Modern Chinese so that they will be able to interact with speakers of Chinese in simple day-to-day situations. A wider range of topics on Chinese society and culture will also be introduced through mini-lectures, audio-visual presentations and real-time classroom-based or online tutorials.

title: Social Work and Mental Health Recovery
description: This unit explores major psychiatric disorders and treatments in adult mental health. Students will investigate psychiatric, psychological, social and recovery discourses that inform social work practice. Students will critically examine power, privilege and professional authority. Engagement, assessment and intervention within the roles and responsibilities of the social worker and the interprofessional team will be explored. Students will assess and explore personal values, cultural belief systems and their impacts in mental health practice.

title: Materials Chemistry
description: Materials Chemistry is an introductory unit covering three topics that combine to present a solid understanding of Materials Chemistry. The topics will cover the structures and properties of materials (such as carbon-based and nano-scale materials) and how these can be synthesised and characterised in the laboratory and simulated using computer modelling.

title: Environmental Chemistry
description: The unit is an advanced chemistry unit which builds upon and expands the knowledge gained in successful completion of pre-requisite units. Topics to be addressed in this unit include: Aquatic Chemistry: chemistry of natural water systems, including oceans, lakes, rivers, groundwater; physical, chemical and aesthetic indicators of water quality and their analytical methods; water systems as resources and implications on water quality. Atmospheric Chemistry: stratospheric ozone chemistry and tropospheric chemical phenomena, including photochemical smog and acid rain; the mechanism of the Greenhouse Effect and global warming. Biogeochemistry: chemistry of sediments, soils, lakes etc., including molecular markers, stable isotopes, PAHs of organic matter; formation of petroleum and its molecular composition. Environmental toxins: chemistry of environmentally toxic compounds, including source, pervasiveness and persistence; detection; and remediation/regulatory practices.

title: Engineering Economics, Management and Sustainability
description: In this unit, you will learn how engineering projects are evaluated, across the life-cycle, using the principles of economics, management, and sustainability by all practicing engineers. Regardless of the discipline of engineering, the core principles learned in this unit will allow you to plan, develop and manage the execution of projects and learn how to deal with risks and uncertainties inherent in managing them. You will learn how to economically ascertain the challenges and associated opportunities in sustainable practices, and how to analyse the impacts of proposed actions through the lens of economics. You will learn how a business may be optimally structured at start-up from both a management and an equity structure standpoint, and how this structure may change over time necessitated by external funding mechanisms including sourcing equity and debt, as well as due to management requirements. You will gain insights into what is involved in being an entrepreneur starting your own business and also as a manager of an existing, established business, both listed and unlisted. Over the duration of the unit, you will start developing a business case for a project or a start-up from week 2. Every week you will provide an update based on principles taught in the previous week. Collectively over 12 weeks, you will have developed a sound business proposal/plan, fully supported with defendable economic imperatives, which you will pitch to potential stakeholders for investment (or non-investment)

title: Microcomputers
description: This unit will examine microcontroller and microcomputer architectures, including von Neumann architecture, instruction sets and memory maps. Methods of input/output and assembly languages will also be covered and demonstrated with the use of integrated development environments (IDE). An introduction to high level languages, such as C, will be used to demonstrate the development process involved in embedded systems

title: Requirements Engineering
description: An introduction to the fundamentals of the software engineering (SE) discipline. The basic concepts to be presented are an understanding of requirements engineering, its scope and its role in software development. Role of requirements. Engineering in SE. An understanding of techniques and tools available for requirement specification. Current techniques, notations, methods, processes and tools used in requirements engineering. An understanding of the role of prototyping in requirements engineering. Gain a basic grounding for research in requirements engineering including current research issues and direction of the field. Awareness of literature.

title: Contemporary Health and Social Issues in Australian Communities
description: This unit explores contemporary health and social issues such as substance use, mental distress, aged care and disability. Critical theories are used to examine how these issues impact on individuals, families and communities. Reforms which influence and frame contemporary social work practice will be analysed. These include health system arrangements, self-directed support in disability and aged care and service integration across various sectors such as health and mental health, housing, employment and education.

title: Complexity and Case Management
description: Students will be able to: explain the origins and organisational determinants of case management practices; describe complexities of living with co-existing health, social and disability challenges; and articulate social work values, ethics, roles and responsibilities in inter-organisational and inter-professional practice. The unit prepares students for beginning social work practice.

title: Working with Communities
description: Students will develop understandings and explanations of the multiple forms of community and examine how practice can be responsive to these diversities. This unit introduces students to theories and practices of working with communities and presents some of the challenges, tensions and possibilities of community practice in local and global contexts. Students will identify, assess and apply knowledge, skills and values for community practice. This unit offers relevant knowledge and practice skills for a range of professional disciplines.

title: Social Work Practice with Children and Young People
description: This unit will explore social constructions of childhood and adolescence. Students will develop the skills to work with children and adolescents. Care contexts will be explored as part of this unit of study. International and Indigenous perspectives will frame the theoretical approaches that underpin this unit. Students will be introduced to child and adolescent mental health with a particular focus on loss and grief; and working with parents.

title: Field Geology Techniques
description: This unit provides a basic introduction to geological maps and stratigraphy, which will be followed by field-based practical geological mapping exercises on the field trip. Skills developed include field geological mapping using aerial photographs, meticulous and comprehensive documentation of observations in field notebooks, and measurement of structural data using a compass clinometer. Work-integrated learning aspects of the unit include the development of a professional attitude to field safety and field camp organisation, and an appreciation of the importance and meaning of rocks in indigenous culture.

title: Integrated Design Project
description: This unit provides students with an opportunity to integrate technical knowledge and generic skills gained over the past three years in the course. The topics that are covered in this unit are: Unit Overview, Project Proposal and Technical Report Writing, Research and Design Methodology, Project Management, Proposal Submission and Presentation, Conceptual Design, Product/Process/System Design, Sustainable Design, Final Project Presentation and Demonstration.

title: Advanced Workplace Writing
description: This unit is designed to introduce students to a range of writing and research tasks common to workplaces in both the public and private sectors. It covers the production of workplace documents (including speeches, briefing notes, website material, media releases and corporate communications) as well as a curriculum vitae and responses to selection criteria. It provides an introduction to research and writing as part of a team as well as an individual activity and introduces students to policy analysis.

title: Porous Media Characterisation
description: The subsurface environment has a crucial role in addressing the challenges of the energy transition in terms of both non-hydrocarbon resources exploration and storage solutions. Porous media characterisation is the process of analysing and describing the physical properties of materials that have interconnected void spaces. The objectives of this unit are for students to become familiar with petrophysical conditions favourable for resources exploration, energy storage, assessment of geothermal sites for heat production; and for petrophysical evaluation of the CO2 and other wastes storage sites. This unit will provide most of the essential parameters required for the characterisation of subsurface porous media using logging tools including an introduction to porous media, identification of the type of porous media, storage capacity estimation, pore size distribution & surface area, capillary pressure, injectivity and deliverability assessment, porous media mechanical properties calculations, volumetric calculations, and uncertainty analysis.

title: Machine Dynamics
description: Machine Dynamics focuses on the fundamental concepts and mathematics of simple dynamics, with some supporting mathematics and common applications. Coordinate systems (with repeated integrals) and vector functions are introduced in the context of relative motion, velocity and acceleration diagrams, in order to analyse planar kinematics of rigid bodies, and rotating and reciprocating components. Newton's Second Law and free body diagrams introduce the link between kinetics and kinematics, along with static and dynamic friction, inclined plane motion, and rigid body motion with applied forces and torques. Mass moments of inertia are calculated for simple and complex bodies using parallel and perpendicular axis theorems. These concepts are applied to simple mechanical power transfer systems including gears (fixed axis and epicyclic) and belt drives (flat and Vee belts). Some applications of first and second order differential equations are introduced.

title: Biomechanics
description: This unit introduces students to the major biomechanical factors involved in movement, with a special focus on locomotion, sports technique, and injury prevention. The material is presented with an emphasis on the analysis of motions and forces acting on and within the human body.

title: Global Public and Planetary Health
description: Human health and the health of the planet are interconnected. In this unit, students will be introduced to key concepts and frameworks for the analysis of global public and planetary health in the context of sustainability and the Sustainable Development Goals. Students will learn about solutions for the political, economic, social, and environmental determinants of healthy human populations and the natural systems on which they depend. Critical issues for sustainability will be explored on a global scale including collective action problems, power, wealth inequality, poverty, nutrition, water and sanitation, urbanisation, climate change, human consumption and production, human rights and gender equity.

title: Geoscience Professional Practice
description: This unit explores the concept of geoscientific information and provides students with research skills to obtain and access this information and effectively communicate results both in written and oral format with academic integrity. It also addresses professional development and ethics, occupational safety, hazard analysis and risk assessment.

title: Publishing Studio
description: This unit provides students with the opportunity to apply their existing knowledge and skills in order to publish real books, by real authors, for real readers. Depending on the books accepted for publication, where these books are in the publishing process, and the skills and interests of individual students, the unit will vary from semester to semester, as well as from student to student. Nonetheless, every student will be involved in at least two of the following publishing processes: acquisitions, editorial, design, print production, digital production, marketing, and sales. Students will also learn about project management, collaborative problem-solving, financial planning, brand development, social media marketing, and more, as these are all required to operate a real publishing house. The skills developed and practised in this unit are transferrable to a wide variety of industries and workplaces. The Work-Integrated Learning (WIL) approach used in this unit represents a blend of curricular and workplace learning – of theory and practice – which is used to achieve outcomes that meet the needs and expectations of both a diverse student body and the diverse industries that employ students majoring in Professional Writing and Publishing.

title: Australians at War
description: This unit provides a historical overview of Australians’ involvement in war from 1788 to the twenty-first century. From conflict on the colonial frontier to the World Wars and subsequent military deployments, the unit analyses how the prospect, outbreak, and aftermath of war have shaped Australian society and the nation’s role on the international stage. The unit also links war with major themes such as decolonisation, memorialisation, trauma, gender, and peace. Students will gain insight into why the decision to go to war remains one of the most important and contested aspects of government and policymaking.

title: Writing on the Web
description: This unit offers you a practically oriented, conceptually-based approach by which you can become more effective in written publishing via digital and social media. It considers how writing can accommodate the re-structured reading that comes from scrolling down, rather than turning a page, together with the non-linear flow that results from hyperlinking. In this unit, students engage in practical online writing tasks, while also gaining a clear understanding of how writing has evolved through digital forms of publishing. Key ideas relating to relevance, credibility, authority and utility in writing for digital and social media are also discussed.

title: Dynamic and Stochastic Simulation and Optimisation
description: This unit focuses on dynamic and stochastic systems and provides a solid foundation in a range of tools applicable to the complex problems arising in industrial modelling and optimisation. The following areas are covered: Dynamic programming: Basic concepts, applications, models and algorithms are investigated with optimal solutions developed and implemented for relevant applications. Queuing models: Basic concepts are covered. Several types of queuing models and their advantages and disadvantages are studied and optimal solutions are derived for each. Simulation: Simulation is a very powerful tool that provides the industrial modeller with the ability to study complex systems in considerable detail. Simulation modelling comprise of three major components: input generation that allows the system to be viewed "in action"; a bookkeeping phase that keeps track of transactions occurring in the system and keeps counters on ongoing processes in order to calculate appropriate performance measures and output analysis that establish the effectiveness of the system's performance. The unit provides the necessary skills to analyse, develop and implement simulation models. Techniques and methodologies used for the effective optimisation of simulations are also studied.

title: Applied Bioscience for Health Instability 1
description: This unit explores pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, diagnosis and applies clinical decision making to support self management of individuals with adverse health events associated with unstable conditions. Introduction to pharmacology. Topics covered include: diabetes, obesity, pain, STDs, infertility and infection; altered healing and mobility, arthritis, anxiety, depression.

title: Clinical Radiation Therapy Practice 6
description: This unit provides authentic radiation therapy professional practice experience in the clinical setting, at the level appropriate for the competent reflective professional. Students will have the opportunity to develop their skills and understanding of leadership.

title: Marine and Energy Geophysics
description: Geophysical technologies and in particular seismic methods are essential for many marine and energy applications. They will remain critical for research and engineering in the transition to the new forms of energy needed for our future. Seismic techniques help in the development of underwater infrastructures plus the safe storage of carbon dioxide. At the same time seismic methods such as side scanning sonar map the marine setting for environmental and engineering applications. Other seismic methods are used to identify whales or submarines in marine settings.

title: International Study Abroad - Community Service
description: A 75 hour community service placement with an approved host organisation and a 20 hour placement in the Curtin Volunteers! John Curtin Weekend Program. These placements will be supported by pre, mid and post placement classes to reflect on learning outcomes. A pre-placement class will introduce concepts and theories to apply in the professional working environment; understanding of Australian workplace culture; and self-assessment practices. Defining a project or identifying responsibilities on the placement and methods for articulating employability skills for a successful placement will be covered. Opportunities are provided to discuss the application of discipline knowledge during the placement. The mid-placement class will enable students the opportunity to report on their progress and contribution to the organisation; identify any constraints or limitations; and reflect on learning outcomes. Sharing experiences with peers and comparing the interpersonal skills required to interact effectively in multicultural environments will be a focus. A post-placement class provides a chance to reflect on their overall experiences. It is an opportunity to identify how their skills and capabilities have been enhanced, and share similarities and differences in Australian workplace culture in comparison to their home country. Planning a pathway forward for exploring how they will continue to enhance and communicate their employability skills and possibly continue to contribute to their community upon returning home is addressed. Toward the end of the class there will be the opportunity to celebrate successes and achievements with the students, workplace supervisors and members of the University community.

title: Medical Imaging Practice 4
description: Positioning theory, patient care, communication, practice techniques, image acquisition and quality assurance relevant to the advanced beginner reflective practitioner. Particular focus includes safe and effective CT and angiography practice and use of contrast.

title: Integrated Musculoskeletal Science
description: This unit builds upon the biopsychosocial approach to musculoskeletal health across the life-span presented in introductory musculoskeletal science. Clinically-orientated anatomy and pathology are applied in the context of individuals with complex musculoskeletal disorders in first-contact primary care settings. Complexity will be presented in terms of the person specific (psychosocial) factors that are in the cases as well as the anatomy and pathophysiology (bio) of the conditions discussed. Evidence-informed, person-centred assessment and management based on a biopsychosocial framework is developed. Information is gathered from the individual using multidimensional screening tools, medical notes / referral letters, medical imaging, observation and physical assessment procedures. Clinical assessment findings are analysed and common patterns of clinical presentation identified. Principles of clinical decision-making about selection, rationalisation and application of treatment and management are considered, focused on evidence-based high-value care to achieve an optimised return to function. Principles include patient-centred education, graded movement exposure, exercise interventions and physical activity programs, manual therapy, facilitating healthy lifestyle behaviours and appropriate referral to other health care practitioners. Effective person-centred verbal and interprofessional digital communication skills are developed in a musculoskeletal context.

title: Introduction to Evaluation in Indigenous Community Program Context
description: In this unit, students will acquire a comprehensive understanding of the definition, types and benefits of evaluation in Indigenous program contexts. Students will also learn about the key concepts of evaluation and explore the role of evaluation in program design, planning, implementation, and determining the outcomes and impact of Indigenous programs. Differences between program logic (the logic model) and the evaluation plan will be discussed.

title: Contemporary Issues in Management
description: This unit provides the knowledge and skills required to develop and defend a research topic and research questions. Students will explore the role and relevance of management theory in the research process, and investigate the application of theory to research problems relating to contemporary issues in management.

title: Applied Theatre
description: This unit examines various approaches to and the production of Applied Theatre works. Working either individually or collaboratively, students will take a multidisciplinary approach to the creation of an Applied Theatre work incorporating the practical skills and processes accumulated during their major and in this unit.

title: Social Work Field Education 1
description: Students will undertake 525 hours social work placement in a range of fields and sites of practice under the supervision of an approved supervisor. Integration and application of theoretical frameworks, social work skills and critically reflective practice are essential elements of the placement. Through the use of supervision students will develop competence in evaluating personal values, professional values, ethics and frameworks into practice. Students will apply self-care strategies and undertake critical examination and evaluation of social work in practice.

title: Essential Skills in Paramedicine
description: This unit introduces the essential non-clinical skills required for paramedic practice. Students will explore psychological, social and cultural factors affecting communication in a healthcare context while also considering the power imbalance in the clinician-patient relationship. Basic vital sign acquisition will be taught, as well as how to integrate this into the initial patient assessment in a paramedic setting. Finally, students will learn the logistical and safety considerations required for safe paramedic practice, including scene assessment, manual handling and extrication skills.

title: Speech Pathology Fieldwork 2
description: In this unit, students will undertake speech pathology clinical practice to develop competency according to Speech Pathology Australia Competency-Based Occupational Standards (CBOS). This unit will facilitate the development of skills in the management of paediatric or adult clients in community, health and/or education settings. Students will be expected to demonstrate competency relative to their stage of their fieldwork progression: They will demonstrate approaching intermediate competency at the end of their first placement and intermediate competency at the end of their second placement.

title: Data Science Honours Dissertation
description: Students will be required to conduct an independent research project under the guidance of a supervisor, resulting in the preparation, submission, presentation and defence of a dissertation. Students will develop research, technical and professional and communication skills, research autonomy and specialised knowledge through a process of inquiry involving the formulation of research questions and hypotheses; selection of appropriate methodology and experimental design; ethical consideration of the research process; critical review of scientific literature; effective scientific writing; development of a project proposal, and the preparation of a dissertation.

title: Applied Public Health Practice
description: This capstone unit prepares students for public health practice, drawing on the skills and knowledge developed over the course of their degree. Students will integrate their learning in the key aspects of public health, and apply these to execute a practical and substantial project. Students will work collaboratively with staff and stakeholders in specific institutions or regions and will develop skills as an effective team member and leader. The focus is on addressing and designing solutions to complex problems using technical and communication skills that will contribute to discipline knowledge and professional practice.

title: Fashion Merchandising
description: This unit will examine the design development for presentation of fashion product in wholesale and retail contexts. The syllabus covers: Industry Trends, Fashion Forecasting, Product Branding, Logo, Swing Tag, business card, Garment Labeling, Industry standards, Fabric composition & Care labelling, Sizing Product display and presentation, Trade shows/Exhibition Stand display Fashion Parade/Event Retail Display – in-store concept and window display.

title: Advertising Design 4
description: A focus on concept and campaign development, professional practice and project management. Students will undertake a series of practical advertising design projects for the purposes of demonstrating skills and competency in advertising design.

title: International Study Abroad 6
description: n/a

title: International Relations Theory
description: This unit introduces students to a series of analytical lenses through which we can observe and interpret events in the international arena that enable a deeper understanding of underlying causes and potential outcomes. It provides a global context for understanding how to evaluate and modify international policy design, enabling students to critically assess the policy choices made by decision-makers, and formulate alternative policy options in the public and private spheres. Topics include realism, liberalism, the English School, constructivism, critical theory, ontological security, Marxism, gender and feminism, environmentalism, and international ethics.

title: Analytics for Observational Data
description: Students will study the principles and practice of modelling and analysing observational data, with an emphasis on practical applications. The core concepts are probability modelling, prediction, and model checking and evaluation. Probability models for various kinds of data are introduced, including models for counts of events, categorical variables, waiting times, and other quantitative and categorical variables. The main focus is on analysing several or many variables, using statistical learning techniques such as correlation, discrimination, principal components and other dimension reduction methods, linear and generalised linear models, regularisation, feature and variable selection, and classification trees. Students taking this unit will be expected to be proficient in the precepts of reproducible research using languages such as R or Python.

title: Renewable Energy Systems
description: This unit prepares a student to design and analyse practical renewable energy systems using energy sources such as solar photovoltaics, wind generators and hydro power generators with the use of power electronic converters and energy storages. Analysing the performance of real-scale renewable energy systems in a hardware laboratory and designing new renewable energy systems using software tools are key components that enhance the knowledge gained through lectures and workshops.

title: A History of Nationalism and Nation-Making
description: This unit examines the history of nationalist thought and nation-states in the modern world. Students learn and critically appraise the main theories of nationalism and how such theories could be applied in understanding nationalist sentiment and the development of nation-states around the world. Students develop the skills to design and carry out a robust research project in History related to the topic of nationalism and nation-states.

title: Social Work with Groups and Families
description: Students will be introduced to the theory, skills and practice of group work. The unit focuses on the development and consolidation of theoretical knowledge and core practical skills in working with and counselling families.

title: Environmental Restoration
description: To better manage natural resources we need to improve our ability to repair the damage caused by past human activities and minimise future damage. This unit introduces the major issues and approaches involved in environmental restoration. The lectures cover a range of topics, from the basic scientific concepts involved in restoration, through a range of examples from different ecosystem types, to the broader social and policy issues involved in implementing restoration. The lectures are supplemented by a series of field visits, workshop and laboratory sessions which provide first-hand experience of techniques and issues.

title: Integrated Pharmacology and Therapeutics 2
description: In this unit, students learn about the pathophysiology, pharmacology and pharmacotherapy for the management of conditions and complications affecting the cardiovascular, renal and endocrine systems and apply current evidence to resolve clinical problems. The unit comprises 4 modules. Module 1: Patient monitoring, including interpretation of laboratory data. Module 2: Cardiovascular disorders including hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cardiac arrhythmias and stroke. Module 3: Acute and chronic renal disorders. Module 4: Conditions associated with the endocrine system including diabetes and contraception.

title: Acting Fundamentals
description: This unit introduces students to foundational skills and processes applicable to a variety of performance contexts, including practice, analysis and reflection. This unit provides a clear framework from which to approach any performance activity.

title: Human Movement Science
description: This unit focuses on developing an understanding of the physiology of normal movement, and how this shapes motor control and motor learning principles. Students will develop their communication skills in instruction and feedback, and their observational skills in the analysis of movement, applying these to problem-solve clinical case vignettes. Physiotherapy handling for functional movement and motor learning practice schedules will be applied in a practical setting.

title: Extended Cyber Security - Intrusion Detection System and Incident Handling
description: This unit introduces the technology behind intrusion detection and examines the approaches taken by intrusion detection systems, both at the network and host level. It examines the differences between using host based and network based IDSs and how each of them can be implemented. Students learn how to analyse the different responses required, depending on the risk/threat to the system and how to handle intrusions. The unit will first examine in detail the different approaches in Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS). Next, the unit will cover how an intrusion detection system responds to an alarm and how to design and deploy an IDS to fit the requirements of differing organisations ranging from small LAN based system to multi-level distributed systems.

title: Immersive Experiences
description: In this unit, students will synthesise their acquired Interaction and UX design knowledge and undertake an advanced and comprehensive Immersive Digital Experience project of their choosing. Through blue-sky thinking and future-oriented projects, students are encouraged to explore, research, collaborate, and challenge the status quo of digital experiences to produce cutting-edge outcomes with industry-grade production and approaches.

title: Studies in Cognitive Neuroscience and Motor Speech Disorders
description: Students will develop foundation knowledge of the anatomy, structure and function of the brain and nervous system as relevant to Speech Pathology. They will critically evaluate the evidence base to plan assessment and intervention for adult speech disorders. Simulated learning will be adopted to ensure students are prepared to work with clients with a motor speech disorder in clinical settings.

title: Advanced 3D Modelling and Digital Fabrication
description: This unit adds value to the creative activities completed in the course. Advanced practices in digital visualisation and fabrication for complex designs show through a portfolio of work, which includes research activities, reflective practice, self-appreciation of abilities and a market appraisal. Activities will consist of completion of keystone work, high-level presentations, showing your knowledge and practical skills in rendering and fabrication techniques to produce professional-level designs using 2D & 3D visualisations and physical modelling.

title: Journalism Major Project
description: The project unit is a culmination of the journalism degree whereby students apply the skills and knowledge learnt over the course of their studies to produce a major journalism project or body of work.Students will take ownership of their work, choosing both the topic and platform/s through which it will be presented, in consultation with supervising staff. Students will apply their research, newsgathering, writing/presentation, technical and problem solving skills to produce a multi-faceted project of their choice. The unit will also focus on developing the entrepreneurial skills necessary for students to engage audiences and convince publishers of their capabilities as an emerging journalist and of the value of their journalism.

title: Clinical Radiation Therapy Practice 5
description: This unit provides authentic radiation therapy professional practice experience in the clinical setting, at the level appropriate for the advanced beginning/competent reflective professional. Students will have the opportunity to reflectively plan for their transition to professional practice.

title: International Theatre
description: Examination of a range of international plays, playwrights and movements in modern and contemporary theatre and contemporary performance from the early twentieth century to the present day as blueprints for: performance; ideological statements and reflections of the historical, cultural and political environment of their creation and production. Critical writing about the plays, playwrights and movements will also be examined.

title: Estate Planning
description: This unit provides an introduction to the legal issues that need to be considered in estate planning including wills, testamentary trusts, taxation of deceased estates, capital gains tax in respect of assets transferred after death, business succession planning and social security.

title: Applied Mathematical Modelling
description: This unit introduces the fundamental techniques and methods for solving real world problems by building mathematical models and fosters a deeper understanding of the use of mathematics in science and engineering disciplines. Topics covered include Newton’s laws and their applications, suffix notation and tensor operations, stress equations of motion, rate of strain tensors and constitutive equations, mathematical modelling of heat transfer and fluid flows, solutions of partial differential equation models in biology, engineering and science, diffusion, water filtration and traffic flow.

title: Advanced Topics in Optimisation
description: This unit introduces the fundamental techniques and methods for solving optimisation and numerical optimisation problems. Topics will cover optimisations models, one-dimensional search techniques, unconstrained optimisation techniques including steepest descent method, Newton’s method, conjugate gradient methods, and constrained optimisation techniques including Lagrangian multipliers, Kuhn-Tucker optimality conditions, sequential quadratic programming.

title: Physical Geodesy
description: This unit covers the role that the Earth’s gravity field plays in geodetic surveying and the gravity-related corrections that are applied to surveying measurements. It defines the anomalous and normal gravity fields and how these are used to compute the geoid via Stokes’s solution of the geodetic boundary-value problem. It covers the subtleties of heights and how they are affected by gravity. It describes the dynamics of the solid Earth and how these time variations affect modern reference frames. General and special relativistic effects on surveying measurements are also covered.

title: Translational Microbiology
description: Microbially produced compounds including antibiotics, enzymes and biofuels play significant roles in global health outcomes and economic progression. The relevance of bacteria to molecular biotechnology is illustrated with examples of medicine, public health, industrial fermentations, bioprospecting, bioremediation, biopesticides, and agriculture applications. The impact of microbiology on human health will be studied by examining interactions between microbial communities and their environment, with emphasis on microbial diversity and their metabolic activities. This interdisciplinary unit will allow students to explore and utilize genetic research, molecular biology, chemistry, and environmental microbiology focusing on how to turn lab based discoveries into tangible solutions for real world issues.

title: Social Work Counselling Individuals
description: This unit will equip students with practical skills and knowledge to apply psychosocial assessments and develop purposeful counselling interactions with individuals. Students will reflect critically on contemporary philosophies, theories and practices. This unit explores the emotional responsiveness and the therapeutic relationship with a focus on planning and goal-setting in counselling.

title: Clinical Microbiology
description: This unit involves the study and discussion of: Infectious diseases affecting various body sites and their differential laboratory diagnosis; the pathogenesis and laboratory features of medically significant micro-organisms, primarily bacteria, with an introduction to parasitology and laboratory instrumentation. A significant discussion of antibacterial agents and antibacterial resistance is incorporated.

title: Law Review
description: This unit enables students to work on one of the Law Reviews that will be edited in the School of Law. In particular, students will become familiar with the process of publishing a law review by corresponding with authors, reviewing and revising submissions and checking references. The unit will also deal with the art of writing legal book reviews.

title: Mathematical Statistics
description: This unit will cover the probabilistic framework for modelling real-world processes. Students will acquire practical skills in developing probability models for processes, compute various probabilities of interest and estimate parameters of the underlying models. There will be a particular emphasis on mathematical-statistical techniques and how these are used to compute probabilities of interest for both discrete and continuous processes.

title: Topics in Sustainable Development
description: Human population growth and the increasing demand for resources is severely impacting management of the natural environmental and conservation of biodiversity. Without actions to reduce the human footprint and develop sustainably, the natural environment will continue to be degraded. This unit enables students to understand and reflect on some of the main sustainability challenges that the world faces now and into the future and to reflect on the relationships between these issues. Major topics include sustainable production and consumption, cities, integration of biodiversity and humanity, and sustainability monitoring. Scientific innovation will be considered alongside advances in policy and monitoring.

title: Clinical Pathophysiology
description: In this unit, students are introduced to pathophysiology of body systems. Students explore incidence and prevalence of acute, chronic and terminal pathology and co-occurring conditions. Aetiology, signs, symptoms and trajectories; medical and surgical investigation, assessment and intervention in common conditions; effect of pharmacological management on health disorders as well as the impact of conditions on people and quality of life, form key learning experiences within the unit.

title: Pharmacology Principles
description: This unit of learning introduces students to essential principles and concepts in the discipline of pharmacology; the field of inquiry dealing with the action of drugs on the human body. Topics that are covered focus on drug action and how the body metabolises and excretes them: molecular mechanisms of drug action on cellular components, also called pharmacodynamics; principles, applications and calculation skills of drug absorption, distribution and elimination, collectively called pharmacokinetics; a range of anti-inflammatory drug groups will be used as exemplars to consolidate these pharmacological principles. This formative material, while introducing students to the science of drugs and medicines, emphasises common mechanisms, processes and concepts rather than describing the complex properties of drugs used and abused in today's society.

title: Medical Radiation Research Project 1
description: Development of skills in searching for research literature, critical evaluation, referencing and preparing a literature review. Planning of a research project and preparation of a research proposal.

title: Advanced Topics in Statistics
description: This unit is designed as an adjunct to the Honours Research Dissertation. Students will further develop their research, technical, professional and communication skills, and specialised knowledge through the exploration of advanced concepts in the field of Mathematical Science.

title: Presentation for Broadcast
description: Under the supervision of academic staff and media industry professionals, students will be introduced to the technical and stylistic elements of voice and on-camera presentation for radio and television news. Weekly instruction and practical sessions in a TV and radio studio, as well as field reporting exercises and the opportunity to shadow professional media presenters, equip students to make a successful transition from university to working broadcast newsroom environments.

title: Korean Intermediate 3
description: This unit is an intermediate level unit suitable for students who have successfully completed Korean for Beginners 2 (KORE1001), or who have an equivalent level of competency, such as ATAR Korean. Taught through interactive and self-directed engaging learning approaches and materials, this unit will enable students to progress their Korean language competency and cultural literacy in various aspects of Korean society and culture to prepare them to live and work in Korea. On successful completion of this unit, students will be able to both read and produce low-intermediate level materials in Korean and gain further confidence in using Korean language in everyday and workplace settings. On successful completion of Korean Intermediate 3 and 4 students will reach a level of competency equivalent to TOPIK (Test of Proficiency in Korean) scale of proficiency upper 2/ lower 3.

title: Social Policy Advocacy and Practice
description: This unit examines and analyses social policy in Australia using forms of critical theory. Students will draw on national and international evidence on social policy developments and practices that drive change. Students will develop the key skills necessary to influence policy change. Application of the practices of advocacy is an essential component of the unit.

title: Australian Theatre
description: This unit examines a range of recent Australian plays and considers them from a number of perspectives: as blueprints for performance; ideological statements and reflections of Australia at various stages of its recent history. The set texts include a diverse range of recent Australian plays and critical writing about Australian theatre. The unit provides the opportunity to research and perform a diverse selection of recent Australian plays, with Nationalist, Indigenous, feminist, gay and lesbian voices among those represented in the selection of scripts.

title: Fundamentals of Surveying
description: This unit covers the theoretical and practical aspects of plane surveying including familiarisation, testing, care, and basic maintenance of modern survey instruments, professional collection of surveying measurements using levels, total stations, and steel-bands. Reduction and verification of plane surveying observations is emphasised. The unit includes comprehensive practical application of levelling operations, traversing and detailed mapping.

title: Molecular Genetics and Cell Biology
description: In this unit, students will explore the fundamental concepts of molecular and cell biology, including the central dogma, traditional Mendelian, and modern molecular genetics. Topics will include DNA structure and replication; regulation of gene transcription; protein synthesis and post-translational modification. Cell structure and function will also be explored. The laboratory component allows students to acquire skills to perform experiments in molecular and cell biology. This unit provides the background knowledge necessary for entry into second year units.

title: Cross Institutional Study (within Australia)
description: Please refer to syllabus for the equivalent course

title: Radiation Therapy Practice 4
description: This unit provides a comprehensive development of the theoretical knowledge and practical skills underpinning advanced beginning radiation therapy practice, including the principles, technology, patient positioning and approaches associated with simulation, planning and treatment. This unit provides further development of the advanced beginning radiation therapist’s capacity for culturally safe person-centred care, effective communication, safe and ethical practice, and reflective thinking.

title: Genetic Engineering
description: Students will be introduced to both theoretical and practical aspects of molecular genetics with a key focus on nuclei acid based technologies. Students will study the principles and applications of: enzymes and cloning vectors, southern blotting, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), genetic libraries, DNA clones and sequencing, and the use of radioactive substances. In addition, students will perform a range of mathematical calculations related to the manipulation and interpretation of laboratory data.

title: Fashion Design and Illustration
description: This unit explores the processes of fashion design and illustration through 2 dimensional media. It provides an introduction to the principles of designing garments for the body and the 2 dimensional presentation of ideas.

title: Complex Midwifery Clinical Practice
description: This unit will further develop midwifery skills and experience. Students develop their midwifery philosophy and further enhance reflective practice. This unit includes experience in woman-centred care as part of midwifery continuity of care practice to include women and babies with complexities, such as eclampsia, cord prolapse and complex emergencies. The Midwife Standards for Practice (2018) inform the scope and purpose of this unit.

title: Feeding and Swallowing Disorders
description: This unit addresses assessment and intervention for swallowing disorders across the lifespan. The relationship of swallowing disorders with other communication disorders is explored.

title: Midwifery Clinical Theory and Practice
description: This capstone unit will consolidate midwifery capabilities though clinical placement to the level of initial entry level midwife. Students will be required to demonstrate clinical skills and theoretical understanding and manage the care of women over the continuum of midwifery care, under the supervision of an experienced midwife. Students will demonstrate knowledge of the care of women from multicultural backgrounds and those with complex problems and the importance of Clinical Governance, quality improvement and the safety of women and babies. The Midwife Standards for Practice (2018) are used to demonstrate that the midwifery student is able to practice collaboratively and interprofessionally as a beginning midwife.

title: Management and Leadership in Pharmacy
description: The role of the pharmacist in pharmacy business management and leadership; management models and strategies within community, hospital and innovative pharmacy services. Research and development of a business plan for an innovative pharmacy service or practice improvement project. Advanced pharmacy management including inter-personal skills for people management, change management, information management, financial and risk management. Industrial relations and regulatory matters pertaining to pharmacy business. Buying and selling a pharmacy. Law, ethics and professionalism in pharmacy management. Collaboration and leadership skills to enhance pharmaceutical services to optimise patient outcomes. Advanced Oral and written communication skills in business management and pharmacy leadership.

title: Japanese Society and Culture
description: This unit explores various aspects of contemporary Japanese society by examining social, cultural and historical contexts. Students will gain knowledge of a wide range of aspects of Japanese culture and society such as; Cos-play, geography and climate, territorial disputes, discrimination, Yasukuni and Japan's constitution, martial arts, whaling, abduction and spying, lost generation, J-pop and Enka, as well as Manga and Anime. Students develop an awareness of a variety of perspectives relating to contemporary Japan, an ability to synthesise research findings, analyse information and present their argument successfully.

title: History of the Interior
description: This interdisciplinary unit explores and debates significant art and design movements across the twentieth and twenty-first centuries in the broader context of significant world events affecting social, political, technological, and economical developments, including indigenous perspectives. The effects of these movements on the shaping and making of the interior is considered at both local and international levels, in particular by deconstructing key methods and processes of design practice.

title: Biopharmaceutical Technology
description: This unit introduces students to the concepts and applications of advanced drug delivery systems utilising biopharmaceutical technology including nanotechnology and recombinant DNA technology for transdermal, intraocular, pulmonary, nasal, controlled release dosage forms and targeted drug delivery systems. Principles and application of cold sterilisation technology in the production of sterile pharmaceutical products. Aseptic transfer as a foundation for complex compounding including IV additives, total parenteral nutrition and cytotoxic drug reconstitution.

title: Foundations of Pharmaceutics
description: This unit introduces students to the pharmaceutical science and formulation of liquid and solid dosage forms Pharmaceutical science aspects: Physicochemical properties of pharmaceutical solids including crystalline form, solubility and distribution. Powder technology including particle size analysis, particle size reduction, powder mixing and drying. Physicochemical properties of pharmaceutical solutions including solvents, effects of pH, buffers, phase rule and phase diagrams. Formulation aspects: Formulation, preparation and evaluation of solid oral dosage forms and pharmaceutical solutions. Principles of preservation, flavouring, colouring and stabilisation of pharmaceutical solutions.

title: Acquired Language and Cognitive Communication Disorders
description: In this unit, students will develop their knowledge and understanding of person- and family-centred approaches to acquired language and cognitive communication disorders, and of theoretical models of language as applied to adult language impairment. Students will critically evaluate the evidence for assessment and management of people who have acquired language and cognitive communication disorders. They will develop their skills in assessment, collaborative goal setting, therapy and management of clients. They will learn about culturally safe practice for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and for clients from a range of culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds. This unit supports students to develop their communication and clinical interaction skills relevant to speech pathology practice, including their ability to advocate for clients within the multidisciplinary team, and to work with families and conversation partners.

title: Advanced Calculus 1
